question.text: Will James Comey have at least two federal criminal cases pending against him on November 13, 2026?
question.resolution_criteria: This question is resolved by the status, as of 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026, of federal district-court criminal dockets naming James Comey as a defendant — principally United States v. Comey, No. 1:26-cr-00229-TNM (D.D.C.) and United States v. Comey, No. 4:26-cr-00016-FL-RN (E.D.N.C.) — as shown in public court records (PACER/CourtListener) or, where those records cannot be accessed, [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions). A federal criminal case counts as pending if a charging document (indictment, superseding indictment, or information) naming Comey as a defendant is on file and the case has not been finally disposed of by a judgment. A case remains pending unless every charging document in it has been dismissed in full; dismissal of only some counts, or a superseding indictment filed under the same case number, leaves it one pending case, and a dismissal order takes effect on its entry even if stayed or later appealed. The question resolves Yes if at least two such cases are pending on that date, counting any federal district-court criminal case against him that is pending then regardless of when it was filed, including a previously dismissed case that has been reinstated or re-charged; it resolves No if one or zero are pending. Proceedings in a U.S. Court of Appeals (including Nos. 25-4673 and 25-4674) are not pending criminal cases for purposes of this question.
question.fine_print: A charging document filed under seal counts as pending provided a corresponding entry appears on the case docket.

research:
As of the latest reporting I could find (through November 2, 2026), Comey still has the same two pending federal district-court criminal cases, D.D.C. and E.D.N.C. Nothing has settled the question yet. The near-term pivot is whether a D.C. grand jury indicts him around November 5.

## 1. Resolution source
- The resolving dockets are D.D.C. No. 1:26-cr-00229-TNM and E.D.N.C. No. 4:26-cr-00016-FL-RN on PACER or CourtListener. I could not read them directly. CourtListener's search page loaded without docket results, and its API returned "401: Authentication credentials were not provided." So I could not confirm the latest docket entries myself. Everything below comes from press reports.

## 2. Current status
- 2026-11-02: Reports still show both cases pending. McFadden took Comey's motion to dismiss "under advisement" with no ruling, and no grand jury outcome had been reported. [WEIS/AP](https://weisradio.com/2026/11/02/judge-hears-arguments-over-james-comeys-request-to-throw-out-latest-doj-allegations-against-him/)
- I found no report of a D.C. indictment, a grand jury refusal to indict (a "no bill"), or a dismissal in either case as of November 3.
- E.D.N.C.: I found no ruling on the four defense motions. Flanagan said in late September that they were "ripe for decision" and has not scheduled oral argument. The next court appearance in that case is in January 2027. [GV Wire/NYT](https://gvwire.com/2026/10/09/the-seashells-case-against-comey-at-a-crossroads/), [ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts/story?id=137706147)

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-11-02: A magistrate judge in D.C., Zia Faruqui, threw out DOJ's October 20 case against former FBI officials Floris and Benavides. He found no probable cause and called the prosecution "weaponization." This is relevant to how D.C. courts and grand juries are treating similar politically charged cases. [HNGN](https://www.hngn.com/articles/273674/20261102/judge-calls-doj-case-against-ex-fbi-officials-weaponization-tosses-it.htm)
- 2026-10-30 hearing in the D.C. case:
  - McFadden asked, "Aren't we getting a little ahead of ourselves?" and cited "very novel issues." He appeared to lean toward the defense reading that the statute requires an "indictment."
  - He said the defense could renew its limitations argument after any indictment is returned.
  - He joked that "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days."
  - He warned DOJ against a "dawn raid" arrest, and the prosecutor said "that won't happen."
  - [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-james-comey-information-espionage-act-hearing/), [NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/james-comey-team-court-seeking-toss-third-doj-case-longtime-trump-foe-rcna606394)
- 2026-10-30: DOJ told the court that evidence is being presented to a grand jury now. A DOJ attorney, Farahnak, said newly found evidence of conduct through April 2017 could extend the charging window by about six months. [Spokesman/AP](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/oct/30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-on-defens/), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/30/politics/comey-motion-hearing-leak-charges)
- Deadline uncertainty:
  - ABC says "next Thursday" (November 5) is technically the government's last day to seek an indictment before the information could be dismissed under the Speedy Trial Act.
  - CBS reports that DOJ had agreed, after an earlier emergency hearing, not to seek an indictment for 30 days. One outlet puts the end of that window around November 8, which would conflict with November 5. I could not resolve the conflict.
  - Background on the law: a Speedy Trial Act dismissal under 18 U.S.C. §3162 can be with or without prejudice, and in practice it is usually triggered by a defense motion.
  - [ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts/story?id=137706147), [NY Sun](https://www.nysun.com/article/charges-against-james-comey-hang-in-balance-as-judge-warns-trump-administration-against-dawn-raid-arrest)
- 2026-10-26: The D.C. case was unsealed: two counts under §793(d) and §793(g). [Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/26/james-comey-national-defense-information-charges), [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/26/james-comey-indictment-national-defense-doj-trump.html)
- E.D. Va. appeal: Wikipedia says Fourth Circuit argument was heard on 2026-09-15 before Diaz, Floyd and Richardson, with no decision yet. That differs from the question's background, which says argument was reported for the week of November 2. Either way, the appeal does not count toward resolution. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecution_of_James_Comey)

## 4. Base rates
- D.C. grand juries have repeatedly refused to indict in politically sensitive cases in 2025 and 2026, and McFadden remarked on it. I found no systematic count of D.C. no-bill rates. [Spokesman/AP](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/oct/30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-on-defens/)
- DOJ's track record against Comey so far: 1 of 3 cases dismissed in the district court (E.D. Va., about two months after indictment). The E.D.N.C. case has been pending about 6 months, with motions undecided for about 5 weeks.
- A ruling from Flanagan within the next 10 days is possible but not signalled. Arraignment and trial are set for January and February 2027.

## 5. Other forecasts
These were fetched by code on 2026-11-03. None of them matches the question exactly.
- Kalshi, "Comey NDI case (D.D.C.) dismissed": before Jan 1, 2027 at 23%; before Jul 1, 2027 at 90%. This is the closest market. Note that it could resolve on dismissal of the information even if a replacement indictment is filed, which would not by itself make this question resolve No.
- Kalshi, "Comey criminal case dismissed" (case not specified): before Jan 1, 2027 at 27%; before Jul 1, 2027 at 63%.
- Polymarket, "Comey charges dropped by Dec 31": 39%.
- Kalshi, "Comey indictment reinstated on appeal before 2027": 6%. Not relevant to district-court counts.
- Polymarket, "Comey sentenced to prison in 2026": 1.2%.
- I found no Metaculus or expert forecast on this exact question.

## 6. Upcoming events before November 13
- About November 5: the reported deadline for a D.C. indictment. Possible outcomes:
  - An indictment is returned. It could be filed under the same case number or as a new case. If it is a new case, the D.C. information and the new indictment could briefly be two separate D.C. cases.
  - A no bill.
  - DOJ misses the deadline, after which the information could be dismissed under the Speedy Trial Act, possibly only on Comey's motion.
- A McFadden ruling on the limitations motion could come at any time, especially after any indictment.
- A Flanagan ruling on the four E.D.N.C. motions could come at any time. Nothing is scheduled.
- November 3, 2026 is midterm Election Day. Some reporting tied DOJ's timing in other cases to the midterms.

## 4. Base rates
- D.C. grand juries have repeatedly refused to indict in politically sensitive cases in 2025-26, as AP noted and McFadden remarked. I found no systematic no-bill rate for D.C.
- In Comey's own prosecutions:
  - The E.D. Va. grand jury returned only some of the proposed counts.
  - The E.D. Va. case was dismissed about two months after indictment.
- Judges rarely dismiss threat cases before trial on true-threat grounds. Courts usually leave that question to a jury, which is DOJ's position here. I found no hard numbers.

forecasts.reasoning:
(a) The outcome is known on November 13, 2026, about 10 days from now. For Yes, at least two federal district-court criminal cases against Comey must be pending at that date. In practice that means the D.D.C. case still has a live charging document (the information or a replacement indictment), and the E.D.N.C. indictment has not been dismissed in full.

(b) Status quo: two cases are pending today, so the status quo is Yes. Neither judge has ruled, and E.D.N.C. has nothing scheduled until January 2027.

(c) Base rate: when a pending federal criminal case has no decision scheduled within a 10-day window, it is rarely dismissed in that window, probably under 5% per case. The D.D.C. case is more fragile because of the November 5 indictment deadline and an openly skeptical judge. A reasonable starting point is about 80% Yes.

(d) Evidence:
- For Yes:
  - As of November 2, both cases are pending. McFadden took the motion "under advisement" and signaled he would wait for an indictment.
  - DOJ says evidence is before a grand jury now. Any indictment, under the same or a new case number, keeps a D.C. case pending.
  - Flanagan has set arraignment and trial for January and February 2027, and has scheduled no oral argument.
  - Kalshi prices dismissal of the D.D.C. case before January 1, 2027 at only 23%. That market counts dismissal even if a replacement indictment follows, so it overstates the risk to this question.
- For No:
  - D.C. grand juries have no-billed politically charged cases in 2025 and 2026. McFadden joked that "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days."
  - On November 2, Magistrate Judge Faruqui tossed the related Floris and Benavides case as "weaponization."
  - McFadden seems to favor Comey's reading that the statute requires an indictment.
  - The November 5 Speedy Trial deadline sits inside the window.

(e) Scenarios:
- No: around November 5 the D.C. grand jury returns a no bill. Comey immediately moves to dismiss, and McFadden dismisses the information by about November 10, calling further proceedings futile. Alternatively, Flanagan grants the true-threat motion.
- Yes: the grand jury indicts, or DOJ keeps presenting evidence while the information stays on file. McFadden defers ruling on the renewed limitations motion, and Flanagan does not rule before November 13.

(f) Moving from the base rate:
- I put the chance of a no bill or a missed deadline at about 35 to 40%.
- Given that, I estimate roughly a 35% chance the information is dismissed within the short 8-day window. That gives about 12% for the D.C. path to No.
- I add about 4% for an E.D.N.C. dismissal in the window.
- Together that is roughly 16 to 18% No, which is consistent with the Kalshi price as an upper bound. I stay close to the status quo prior.

Probability: 82%

(a) **Time left and what Yes requires.** About 10 days remain, until 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026. Yes requires that at least two federal district-court criminal cases with a live charging document are pending against Comey on that date. In practice that means both the D.D.C. and E.D.N.C. cases survive. An alternative path is that the D.C. charge is replaced by a new indictment filed as a separate case.

(b) **Status quo.** Two cases are pending today, so nothing changing means Yes. McFadden has the limitations motion under advisement. Flanagan has four ripe motions and no hearing set, and her next appearance in the case is January 2027.

(c) **Base rate.** Federal criminal cases rarely get disposed of within an arbitrary 10-day window. The exception is a hard procedural deadline falling inside that window, which is the case here. For a typical pending case, 10-day survival is above 95%. For two cases with one facing a deadline, a reasonable starting point is about 85% Yes.

(d) **Strongest evidence.**

For Yes:
- DOJ said on Oct 30 that it is actively presenting evidence to a D.C. grand jury and has new evidence of conduct through April 2017.
- McFadden signaled on Oct 30 that he would wait for an indictment, and said the limitations issue could be renewed afterward. That points away from a quick ruling.
- Kalshi prices D.D.C. dismissal before Jan 1, 2027 at only 23%. That market even counts dismissal of the information when it is replaced, so dismissal within 10 days is implied to be well under 23%.
- Flanagan shows no sign of ruling soon.

For No:
- D.C. grand juries have repeatedly returned no bills in politically charged cases, and McFadden joked about it.
- On Nov 2, Magistrate Faruqui tossed the Floris/Benavides case for lack of probable cause.
- The reported Speedy Trial Act deadline is Nov 5. A no bill, or a missed deadline, could prompt a quick dismissal motion that McFadden is already primed to grant.

(e) **Scenarios.**
- **No:** The grand jury no-bills Comey around Nov 5. Comey moves to dismiss under the Speedy Trial Act and on limitations, and McFadden dismisses the information around Nov 10-12, or DOJ drops it. Only the E.D.N.C. case remains.
- **Yes:** The grand jury indicts, either as a superseding indictment in the same docket or as a new case. Alternatively, a no bill occurs but the dismissal ruling slips past Nov 13. Either way, the E.D.N.C. motions stay pending.

(f) **From base rate to final probability.** I start from about 85% and adjust down for the D.C. deadline risk.
- I put a no bill or missed deadline at roughly 35-40%.
- Given that, I put a dismissal actually entered by Nov 13 at about 40-50%. That gives roughly 15-18% for the D.C. case dropping out.
- I add about 5-6% for an E.D.N.C. dismissal in the window, or a sudden limitations ruling in D.C.

Total No risk is about 22%, which is consistent with the Kalshi signal.

Probability: 77%

**(a) Time left and what Yes requires.** The outcome is known about 10 days from now, at 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026. Yes requires that both the D.D.C. case and the E.D.N.C. case (or a replacement case) still have a charging document on file that has not been dismissed in full. A new D.C. indictment, under the same case number or a new one, keeps the D.C. side pending.

**(b) Status quo.** Both cases are pending as of November 2, so the status quo outcome is Yes.

**(c) Base rate.** In politically charged federal cases with dismissal motions pending, a dismissal arriving within a specific 10-day window is uncommon. I would put the chance that both cases simply survive such a window at about 85-90%. The D.C. case has an unusual scheduled pivot around November 5, which lowers this somewhat.

**(d) Strongest evidence.**
- *For Yes:*
  - DOJ said on October 30 that evidence is before a grand jury now and that newly found conduct through April 2017 extends the charging window.
  - McFadden said the defense could renew its limitations argument after any indictment, which suggests he expects to let the indictment route play out rather than rule now.
  - Flanagan has scheduled nothing before January 2027.
  - Kalshi puts dismissal of the D.D.C. case before January 1, 2027 at only 23%. That market also counts dismissal of the information even when a replacement indictment follows.
- *For No:*
  - D.C. grand juries have repeatedly refused to indict in 2025-26, and McFadden joked that "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days."
  - On November 2, magistrate judge Faruqui threw out the Floris/Benavides case as "weaponization."
  - McFadden appeared skeptical of the information approach and said a refusal to indict would make the proceedings futile.
  - The four E.D.N.C. motions have been ripe since late September.

**(e) Scenarios.**
- *No:* The grand jury returns a no bill around November 5. Comey immediately renews his motion, and McFadden dismisses the information under the Speedy Trial Act or on the limitations argument by around November 12, leaving only the E.D.N.C. case. A less likely No route is Flanagan granting the First Amendment or vindictive-prosecution motion this week.
- *Yes:* The grand jury indicts, or DOJ keeps the information alive while it re-presents. McFadden takes renewed motions on a briefing schedule that runs past November 13, and Flanagan stays silent.

**(f) Moving to a final number.**
- I estimate about a 60% chance the D.C. grand jury indicts by the deadline.
- If it does not, I give about a 50% chance McFadden actually enters a dismissal before November 13, since judges often need briefing and DOJ may argue the clock is different. That makes a D.C.-driven No about 20%. Cross-checking against Kalshi, which implies maybe 10-15% for dismissal of any kind by mid-November, I shade this down to about 14%.
- I add about 5% for an E.D.N.C. dismissal in the window.
- Total P(No) is about 18-19%, so I move from the roughly 87% base rate down to about 81%.

Probability: 81%

**(a) Time left and what Yes requires.** About 10 days remain, to 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026. Yes requires that, on that date, both the D.D.C. case (an information, or a replacement indictment under any case number) and the E.D.N.C. indictment are still on file and not dismissed in full.

**(b) Status quo.** Two cases are pending today, so the status quo is Yes. Courts move slowly, and dismissal orders usually take weeks.

**(c) Base rate.** Over a 10-day window, two pending federal criminal cases with ripe dismissal motions both usually survive. The chance a given ripe motion is granted within a specific 10-day window is low, perhaps 5-10% per case. The D.C. case is unusual because of the hard November 5 deadline, so I use a starting point of about 80% Yes.

**(d) Strongest evidence.**

For No:
- On October 30, McFadden was skeptical of using an information to stop the limitations clock.
- ABC reported that November 5 is the Speedy Trial deadline for an indictment.
- D.C. grand juries have returned repeated no-bills in politically charged cases. McFadden joked that "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days."
- On November 2-3, Judge Faruqui tossed the Floris/Benavides case as "weaponization," showing D.C. courts are hostile to these prosecutions.

For Yes:
- DOJ says it has gathered more evidence and has subpoenaed a Comey adviser.
- Conduct running through April 2017 could extend the limitations window into 2027, so DOJ can re-indict later.
- Even if the deadline passes, dismissal needs a defense motion and a court order, which takes time.
- Kalshi prices D.C. dismissal before January 1, 2027 at only 0.23. That market likely counts a dismissal-plus-replacement as "dismissed," which our question would not.
- The E.D.N.C. motions were undecided in late October. Flanagan has set a slow schedule, with trial in 2027, and pretrial true-threat dismissals are rare.

**(e) Scenarios.**
- No: the D.C. grand jury returns a no-bill or DOJ misses November 5. Comey moves immediately, and McFadden dismisses the information on Speedy Trial or limitations grounds around November 10.
